# Diagnosing High CO Emissions on Older Toyota Yaris Models

A rising Carbon Monoxide (CO) reading paired with a P0172 "System Too Rich" code points to a specific combustion imbalance: excess fuel relative to oxygen. When the engine control unit (ECU) detects this condition, it typically attempts to compensate by enriching the mixture further or retarding ignition timing, which often exacerbates the problem rather than solving it. In the context of a 19-year-old Toyota Yaris, where you report smelling petrol upon startup and after driving, the root cause is almost certainly an intake air leak or a failing evaporative emission control system (EVAP), not necessarily a dead catalytic converter.

The P0172 code indicates that the upstream oxygen sensor (O2S) in Bank 1 is reporting a voltage pattern consistent with a rich mixture. The ECU interprets this as "too much fuel" and tries to lean out the mix by cutting fuel injection or enriching the air, but if the leak persists, it cannot compensate. This creates a feedback loop that drives CO emissions up. While the MOT report shows Hydrocarbons (HC) and Lambda values are currently within limits, HC is often the first metric to spike when a catalyst fails completely; however, CO rises significantly when the air-fuel ratio leans out of the stoichiometric window due to unmeasured air entering the intake manifold.

Smelling petrol on startup or after driving suggests fuel is vaporizing into the cabin or leaking into the atmosphere through the crankcase ventilation system or the EVAP purge valve. If the charcoal canister in the EVAP system is saturated with fuel vapors and the purge solenoid is stuck open, it will draw raw fuel vapors directly into the intake manifold during idle and low-load conditions. This acts exactly like an unmetered air leak but delivers hydrocarbons instead of nitrogen. The ECU sees a sudden spike in mass airflow from this vapor intrusion, miscalculates the mixture, and injects more fuel to match the perceived load, resulting in a rich condition and high CO output.

Before condemning the catalytic converter, you must rule out intake leaks and EVAP issues. A common pitfall is assuming that because HC is normal, the catalyst is fine. However, modern three-way catalysts have a "thermal window" where they function efficiently only within a very narrow air-fuel ratio range (14.7:1 Â± 0.2). If the mixture is consistently rich due to an intake leak or vapor intrusion, the catalyst will run cold and inefficient, eventually failing to reduce CO effectively even if its internal honeycomb structure is intact.

To diagnose this systematically, inspect the intake manifold gaskets, the brake booster vacuum hose, and the PCV system for cracks or loose clamps. These areas are prone to degradation in high-mileage vehicles. Additionally, verify the operation of the EVAP purge solenoid with a multimeter; if it remains closed when the engine is warm and under load, vapors will not be purged. If the purge valve is stuck open, replace it immediately. Cleaning the MAF sensor helps, but it cannot fix a physical leak in the plumbing. Only after ensuring all intake paths are sealed and the EVAP system is functioning correctly should you consider replacing the catalytic converter, which would likely be a costly last resort rather than the primary solution.
